maths.problem: In the coast test, the 4 cm strip took 5 steps along the Gujarat coast. The 1 cm strip took 31 steps. How long was the coast each time? How much longer was it with the short strip?
maths.answer: 20 cm and 31 cm. The short strip gave 11 cm more.
maths.explain: With the 4 cm strip, 5 steps of 4 cm is 5 × 4 = 20 cm. With the 1 cm strip, 31 steps of 1 cm is 31 cm. 31 − 20 = 11 cm more.
maths.context: This is about the coast test, where you stepped card strips along a coast on a map.
maths.why_maths: Steps are equal groups, so multiplying turns a count of steps into a length we can compare.

maths.problem: On the map, 1 cm stands for 100 km. The Gujarat coast measured 20 cm with the long strip and 31 cm with the short strip. How long is the real coast each time?
maths.answer: 2,000 km with the long strip and 3,100 km with the short strip.
maths.explain: Each centimetre stands for 100 km. 20 × 100 = 2,000 km. 31 × 100 = 3,100 km. The real coast did not change, but the number did, because of the step.
maths.context: This is about the coast test. A map is drawn smaller than the real land, and its scale tells you how much smaller.
maths.why_maths: A map's scale turns centimetres on paper into kilometres of real coast, and shows how big the difference really is.

maths.problem: A drawn tree splits every branch into two. Write the number of branch tips after 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 splits. What is the rule?
maths.answer: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Each number is double the one before.
maths.explain: One trunk splits into 2. Each of those splits into 2, making 4. Then 8, 16 and 32. Each time, every tip becomes two.
maths.context: This is about the fractal tree you drew, where every branch splits into two shorter branches.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the doubling rule lets you predict the next level without drawing it.

maths.problem: The Fibonacci numbers go 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. A big sunflower can show 34 spirals one way and 55 the other. Write the numbers between 13 and 34, and check that 34 + 55 gives the next one.
maths.explain: 8 + 13 = 21. 13 + 21 = 34. 21 + 34 = 55. 34 + 55 = 89. Each number is the two before it added together.
maths.context: This is about the spiral rows on pineapples and sunflowers, which you can count.
maths.why_maths: The adding rule lets you check whether a count you made fits the pattern, or whether to count again.

maths.problem: The Sierpinski triangle has 1 coloured triangle, then 3, then 9. Draw the next shape in your mind. How many coloured triangles are at level 4 and level 5?
maths.explain: Each coloured triangle turns into 3 smaller ones. 9 × 3 = 27. 27 × 3 = 81.
maths.context: This is about the triangle of triangles you drew, where each coloured triangle has its middle left white.

maths.problem: Each time Pavithra halves her strip, the coast measures a bit longer. If the coast had bends at every size forever, would the length ever stop growing?
maths.answer: No. A coast with bends at every size would keep getting longer, without end.
maths.explain: Each shorter strip finds more bends to go into, so it adds more length. If there were always smaller bends, there would always be more to add, so the length would never stop growing. Real coasts stop at the size of sand grains and smaller bits.
maths.context: This is about the coast test, where shorter strips gave longer coasts.
maths.why_maths: Thinking about what happens forever helps us understand why a fractal's length has no top limit.

roots.context: We have learned that a cauliflower, a fern and a coast have patterns inside patterns, and that a coast measures longer with a shorter ruler. Now we ask what these patterns tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: On your map, the 1 cm strip gave a longer coast than the 4 cm strip. It went into small bays that the long strip stepped across. A coast has bends inside bends, down to the grains of sand. So a coast has no single length until we choose the size of our step.
deep_truth.habit: We think every object has one true size, waiting to be measured. A bendy edge shows that its length also depends on how closely we look, so a number is only complete when it says how it was measured.
deep_truth.evidence: In the coast test, the 4 cm strip, the 1 cm strip and the thread gave three different lengths for the same coast of Gujarat. Kerala's smooth coast changed much less. India's official coastline grew from about 7,516 km to about 11,098 km when it was measured on more detailed maps.

three.who_am_i: Your lungs and blood vessels branch inside you, again and again, so that air and blood reach every part of your body.
three.what_is_life: A fern, a sunflower and a snail each solve their own problem by repeating one simple step as they grow.
three.what_is_this_world: Coasts, rivers, clouds and lightning have bends and branches at many sizes, so the world looks different at every distance you look from.

roots.thread: A whole fern grows from one step repeated: make a leaflet, and on that leaflet make smaller leaflets. A sunflower's spirals grow from one turn, repeated hundreds of times. A coast's bends come from waves and rivers wearing at it, again and again, at every size. So the great variety of shapes we see often comes from a few simple steps, each repeated many times.

science.text: The measured length of a coast or border grows as the measuring step gets shorter. Richardson found it, and Mandelbrot explained it in 1967.
Many plants place each new seed or leaf about 137 and a half degrees round from the last, which packs them well and makes Fibonacci spirals.

other_view.view: A coast does have a length for any one map scale, and that is all we need for maps and ships. Saying it has no single length is a puzzle about words, not a deep fact about the world. And a fern repeating its shape a few times is just how ferns grow. It is beautiful, but it carries no lesson about wholeness.

how_we_found_out.story: Lewis Fry Richardson was an English scientist who hated war. In the 1940s he asked a question: do countries with longer borders fight more wars? To find out, he needed the lengths of borders. He looked them up in reference books and found a problem. Spain said its border with Portugal was 987 kilometres long. Portugal said the same border was 1,214 kilometres long. Most people assumed that one country had simply made a mistake. Richardson measured coasts and borders on maps himself. He stepped along them with a measuring tool set to a long step, then a shorter one, then shorter again. Every time the step got shorter, the length got longer, and bendier lines grew faster. Neither country was wrong. They had measured with different steps. His work was published in 1961, after he died. In 1967, Benoit Mandelbrot used it in a paper called 'How Long Is the Coast of Britain?'. In 1975, he named such shapes fractals.
how_we_found_out.who: Lewis Fry Richardson, an English scientist, and Benoit Mandelbrot, a mathematician
how_we_found_out.when: Richardson's measurements in the 1940s and 1950s, published in 1961, and Mandelbrot's paper in 1967
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought every border and coast has one true length, so two different numbers meant someone had made a mistake. Richardson showed that the measured length grows as the measuring step shrinks, so both numbers can be right.
